Ever heard of Dolby? Not so long ago, next to the ubiquitous Intel Inside sticker on a laptop, you would often see the DOLBY logo as well. That alone tells you how much weight this company carries: it is the heavyweight of audio standards, the Qualcomm of the audio world. Now, to pay less Dolby tax, or none at all, someone is taking on the giant by building an open-source ecosystem, and start-ups are joining in.

Samsung and Google challenge Dolby Atmos with Eclipsa Audio

Samsung and Google have joined forces to take on Dolby, the giant of immersive audio. The two companies have announced Eclipsa Audio, a new open-source spatial audio format designed to bring 3D sound to YouTube and to Samsung’s latest TVs and soundbars.

For years Dolby Atmos has been the dominant force in 3D audio, famous for its immersive surround sound. Today almost every major TV maker pays a “Dolby tax” to license Atmos for its premium TVs and speaker systems.

Samsung and Google, however, are trying to change that with the royalty-free Eclipsa Audio. According to Samsung, Eclipsa Audio works much like Atmos, adjusting audio data such as position, intensity and spatial reflections to create 3D sound. The key difference is that it is an open standard, which means hardware makers pay no licensing fees.

The two companies are also working with South Korea’s Telecommunications Technology Association on a certification program to ensure consistent quality across devices that use the technology. Jim Bankoski, Google’s vice president of engineering for Chrome, said the companies believe Eclipsa Audio has the potential to change the way we experience sound, and that they look forward to seeing how the creator community uses it to build new and innovative audio experiences.

Pozalabs and aespa show off an immersive 3D audio experience powered by Eclipsa Audio at CES 2025

At CES 2025, the AI audio start-up Pozalabs demonstrated a breakthrough audio technology that uses Google and Samsung’s Eclipsa Audio format to give the music of K-pop girl group aespa an entirely new immersive dimension.

The technology shows what Eclipsa Audio can do for music production and live performance. With precise control over where sounds sit in space and how they move, listeners can experience a degree of immersion in music never heard before. The demo featured aespa hits remixed to make full use of Eclipsa Audio’s 3D audio capabilities.

Pozalabs’ chief technology officer said that Eclipsa Audio gives music producers and artists an exciting new platform for creating more immersive and engaging listening experiences, and that the collaboration with aespa shows the technology’s enormous potential in pop music.


Do you think Dolby is about to be knocked off its pedestal? Tell me what you think in the comments!
